tone_statements.citation: Kullavanijaya, Pranee & Theraphan L-Thongkum. 1998. Linguistic criteria for determining Tai ethnic groups: Case studies on Central and South-western Tais. In Somsonge Burusphat (ed.), Proceedings of the International Conference on Tai Studies (Bangkok, July 29-31, 1998), 273-298. Bangkok: Institute of Language and Culture for Rural Development, Mahidol University.
tone_statements.quote: Eighteen SWT speaking groups have been found, sixteen out of eighteen speak P-group (*b > p) dialects: Tai Yuan, Tai Khuen, Tai Luang (Tai Yai), Tai Lue, Tai Don/Lon (Tai Khao or White Tai), Tai Dam (Black Tai), Tai Daeng A and B (Red Tai), Tai Moei, Tai Phoeng, Tai Nuea, Tai Heu, Tai Tsang, Tai Tsung, Tai Ya, Tai Eulai/Tai Kha, and Tai Payi (Pa Di in Vietnamese). [...] [p. 283:] Tai Luang (Tat Yai), Tat Payi, Tai Tsang, Tai Tsung, and Tai Ya belong to the same subgroup based on the pattern of tone splits and mergers, i.e. A1-23-4, B123-4, C123-4, where B4 also merges with C123.
tone_statements.locator: p. 279 (section 4; opening paragraph) and p. 283 (first paragraph after the Tai Nuea/Tai Heu examples); tone-split figures on pp. 280-282
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A; Gregerson, Kenneth J; Nguyen Van Loi. n.d. [c. 2000]. Borderlands: Lesser Known Indigenous Languages of Northern Vietnam -- Map & Language Descriptions (University of Texas at Arlington project web page; the Internet Archive 2015 capture).
sources.note: Nothing. Section 'P. Padi [pa31 zi31]' says Padi is a SW Tai language of Muong Khuong (Lao Cai), ~300 speakers, 'in terms of tone splits, tone values, phonology, and lexicon coincidentally very similar to Central Thai of Bangkok'; cites Abadie 1924 and L-Thongkum (1998) for varieties in China. No word-stress statement.

sources.note: Tai Payi is one of 16 P-group (*b > p) North-Southwestern Tai dialects surveyed; by the pattern of Proto-Tai tone splits and mergers it groups with Tai Luang (Shan), Tai Tsang, Tai Tsung and Tai Ya: A1-23-4, B123-4, C123-4 with B4 merging into C123 (Figure 3-4, p. 281-283); Tai Payi is then separated from Tai Tsang/Tsung/Ya by segmental correspondences (d-, b-, ia retained), with tone-marked cognate forms (e.g. Payi dam 'black', baan 'village', xaa 'leg'; tone digits poorly scanned). Tone contrast is presupposed throughout (Gedney tone-box survey); no explicit tone count sentence in the pages…
